_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss in another section (Bethany's short episodes vs Ravi's long ones; Esther's knitting vs Ravi's running). Used by the Part 7 practice page.
title: Science in your ears
subtitle: Four listeners review the science podcasts they can't stop recommending.

sections.A: Bethany, 45, bus driver, on 'Small Wonders'. This podcast is about creatures most people never notice: woodlice, moulds, the bacteria living on your phone. I listen on my breaks between routes, and I've learned more biology in a year than I did in five at school. The two presenters, a professor and a former stand-up comedian, are brilliant together, mainly because they constantly disagree. She'll explain something carefully, and he'll say 'But why would a slug do that?' and they'll argue happily for ten minutes. That's the best bit for me. My only complaint is that each episode lasts barely twenty minutes, and I'm always left wanting another half an hour. I've also become a slightly annoying passenger in other people's cars; my sister no longer lets me talk about fungus on long journeys. Give it a try, though. Start with the episode about ants.
sections.B: Jonah, 17, sixth-form student, on 'The Bang Sunday'. I started listening because my physics teacher mentioned it, and I'm not exaggerating when I say it got me through my exams. The presenter has this gift for explaining really complicated ideas, like black holes or quantum tunnelling, without a single equation, and suddenly the maths in my textbook made sense too. Last month I told my parents I want to study astrophysics at university, which was not the plan a year ago, and I'd honestly put that down to this show. I do have one criticism. Every few minutes there's a whooshing sound effect, presumably to make the science seem dramatic, and it drives me mad. A black hole doesn't need sound effects; it's already the most dramatic thing in the universe. Apart from that, it's perfect, and every episode is free.
sections.C: Esther, 70, retired nurse, on 'Inside Out'. My grandchildren set this up on my tablet last Christmas, and I've barely stopped listening since. Each episode tells the story of a medical discovery, from anaesthetic to the first heart transplant, and the research behind it is excellent. I usually listen with my knitting in the afternoon; I've finished three jumpers and most of the history of medicine. It's rare that I can catch them out, but there was one episode about nursing in the 1950s where they said something I knew was completely wrong, because I was there. I sent them a polite email, and to my surprise they read it out at the start of the following week's programme and apologised. I felt like a celebrity. It's thoughtful, it's never patronising, and it treats its listeners as intelligent people.
sections.D: Ravi, 33, software developer, on 'Deep Field'. This is a podcast about astronomy, and the episodes are long, often two hours, which I love. I listen on my evening runs, and an episode about the birth of stars is the perfect company for a long one by the canal. The host has the calmest voice I've ever heard, almost too calm, to be honest. If I listen in bed, I'm usually asleep within twenty minutes and have to go back the next day to find out what happened to the galaxy. My advice to newcomers would be not to start with the latest episodes, which assume you already know quite a lot. Go back to the first series, from about five years ago, where everything's explained from the very beginning. After that, you'll be hooked, and you'll never look at the night sky in quite the same way.

questions.question: Which person would like each episode to go on for longer?
questions.why: 'Each episode lasts barely twenty minutes, and I'm always left wanting another half an hour.' Ravi's episodes are already two hours long.

questions.question: Which person was introduced to their podcast by younger family members?
questions.why: 'My grandchildren set this up on my tablet.' Jonah heard about his from a teacher.

questions.question: Which person says their podcast has changed their plans for the future?
questions.why: He now wants 'to study astrophysics at university, which was not the plan a year ago'.

questions.question: Which person sometimes misses parts of episodes because they fall asleep?
questions.why: 'I'm usually asleep within twenty minutes and have to go back the next day.'

questions.question: Which person particularly enjoys the arguments between the presenters?
questions.why: 'They constantly disagree… That's the best bit for me.'

questions.question: Which person pointed out an error to the programme makers?
questions.why: She heard something 'completely wrong' and 'sent them a polite email'.

questions.question: Which person is irritated by one feature of the way their podcast is produced?
questions.why: 'There's a whooshing sound effect… and it drives me mad.' Bethany's complaint is about length, not production.

questions.question: Which person listens while doing exercise?
questions.why: 'I listen on my evening runs.' Esther listens while knitting, which is not exercise.

questions.question: Which person found their podcast helpful for their schoolwork?
questions.why: 'It got me through my exams… the maths in my textbook made sense too.' Bethany learned biology, but not for any course.

questions.question: Which person recommends where new listeners should start?
questions.why: 'Go back to the first series… where everything's explained from the very beginning.' Bethany also names an episode, but only briefly; Ravi explains why beginners should start early.
